title: Escalation Standard
summary: Every therapist is expected to escalate concerns, blockers, incidents, misunderstandings, breaches of standards, and client issues through the appropriate leadership channel — early, calmly, and factually.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, every therapist is expected to escalate concerns, blockers, incidents, misunderstandings, breaches of standards, client issues, and situations requiring guidance through the appropriate leadership channel.
Escalation means bringing an issue to the attention of the person who has the responsibility, authority, experience, or position to help resolve it.
At Zura Spa, escalation is not weakness. It is not gossip. It is not "reporting somebody" simply to get them into trouble. It is not avoiding personal responsibility.
Escalation is a professional tool for clarification, protection, problem-solving, accountability, support, and maintaining standards.
If something is affecting the client, the team, the work, the standard, or my ability to perform properly, the appropriate person should know.
We would rather have an issue raised early and resolved than hidden until it becomes a larger problem.

sections.title: 1. Relevance of the Escalation Standard
paragraphs: Escalation supports early problem-solving, client protection, therapist protection, maintaining standards, preventing assumptions, clear accountability, and better team communication.

sections.title: Early Problem-Solving
paragraphs: Small problems are usually easier to solve than large ones.

A therapist should not wait until a client complains seriously, two therapists begin fighting, a routine repeatedly fails, equipment becomes unusable, a misunderstanding spreads, or a standard is repeatedly ignored before informing someone.
Raise problems while they are still manageable.

sections.title: Client Protection
paragraphs: Any situation affecting a client's safety, comfort, privacy, dignity, service quality, professional boundaries, or experience must receive appropriate attention.
The client's experience should never be compromised because a therapist was afraid to speak.

sections.title: Therapist Protection
paragraphs: Escalation also protects therapists. A therapist may encounter an inappropriate client, an accusation, a misunderstanding, a difficult co-therapist, a situation outside their authority, an instruction they do not understand, or a circumstance that makes them uncomfortable.
Reporting the matter creates clarity and allows leadership to support the therapist appropriately.

sections.title: Maintaining Standards
paragraphs: Standards only work when breaches are noticed, communicated, and corrected.
If therapists see standards being repeatedly ignored but nobody communicates it, poor behaviour gradually becomes normal.

sections.title: Preventing Assumptions
paragraphs: When a therapist is uncertain about a routine, a policy, an instruction, a client request, or a leadership decision, they should clarify instead of guessing.
If you do not understand, ask. If you are unsure, clarify. If you cannot resolve it, escalate.

sections.title: Clear Accountability
paragraphs: Escalation ensures that decisions reach the person who actually has the authority to make them.

Therapists should not independently make decisions involving refunds, discounts, compensation, client disputes, serious complaints, policy exceptions, disciplinary matters, or significant safety concerns unless specifically authorized.

sections.title: Better Team Communication
paragraphs: A good escalation culture prevents information gaps, silent resentment, hidden problems, surprises, and unnecessary conflict.
The right people know what is happening and can respond appropriately.

sections.title: 2. The Escalation Mindset
paragraphs: The therapist's mindset should be: "I am escalating because I want clarity, support or resolution — not because I want drama."
A mature escalation should be calm, factual, timely, respectful, relevant, and solution-focused.

sections.title: 3. Escalation Does Not Replace Problem-Solving
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, therapists are expected to have both a problem-solving mindset and an escalation mindset. They work together.
Problem-solving asks: "What can I responsibly do?" Escalation asks: "Who needs to know or become involved?"

A therapist should not escalate every basic task simply to avoid thinking or taking responsibility. But equally, a therapist should not try to personally solve matters that require leadership involvement.
SOLVE WHAT YOU CAN RESPONSIBLY SOLVE. ESCALATE WHAT REQUIRES GUIDANCE, AUTHORITY, SUPPORT OR VISIBILITY.

sections.title: 4. The Simple Rule
paragraphs: When something is affecting CLIENT → STANDARD → SAFETY → TEAM → WORK → CLARITY and you cannot fully or appropriately resolve it yourself: ESCALATE.
And when you are genuinely unsure: Do not guess. Ask or escalate.

sections.title: 5. What Should Be Escalated — Client-Related Issues
list: A client makes an inappropriate request.
A client becomes aggressive or threatening.
A client repeatedly ignores a professional boundary.
A client makes a serious complaint.
A client asks for a refund or discount outside the therapist's authority.
A client reports an injury or serious discomfort.
The therapist is uncertain whether a session should continue.
A client's behaviour makes the therapist uncomfortable.
A privacy or confidentiality concern arises.
Something unusual occurs during the session that leadership should know.

sections.title: Routine and Standard Issues
paragraphs: Escalate when you do not understand a routine or policy, you receive conflicting instructions, you are unsure how a standard should be applied, another therapist repeatedly disregards a routine or openly refuses to follow a standard, you observe a serious breach of professional conduct, or you discover that a process is creating repeated problems.
Do not invent your own interpretation when clarification is available.

sections.title: 6. Escalating Blockers
paragraphs: A blocker is anything preventing a therapist from properly performing their responsibility.

Examples: Required equipment is unavailable. Required supplies have finished. A room cannot be used. A client handover is incomplete. An instruction is unclear. Another dependent task has not been completed. A therapist cannot proceed safely. A schedule conflict prevents proper service.
The therapist should not simply stop working and say "I couldn't do it."
The appropriate response is: "This is what is preventing me from proceeding, this is what I have tried, and this is the support I need."

sections.title: 7. Escalating Misunderstandings
paragraphs: When there is a misunderstanding between therapists, first where appropriate: remain calm, clarify what happened, communicate respectfully, and attempt reasonable resolution.
If the issue cannot be resolved professionally, escalate it.
Do not allow a misunderstanding to develop into silent hostility, insults, refusal to work together, gossip, sabotage, or poor client service.

sections.title: 8. When You Feel Offended or Confronted
paragraphs: Feeling offended does not automatically mean someone has committed misconduct. But neither should therapists allow serious issues to remain unresolved.

If another therapist insults you, humiliates you, threatens you, repeatedly speaks disrespectfully, confronts you aggressively, or interferes with your ability to work, do not create another confrontation.
Where appropriate: Pause → Clarify → Attempt respectful resolution → Escalate if unresolved or serious.
If the behaviour is threatening, unsafe, or serious, escalation should be immediate.

sections.title: 9. When Another Therapist Flouts a Standard
paragraphs: Therapists should not ignore serious or repeated violations simply because "It is not my business." The standard belongs to the entire team.
Where appropriate, a colleague may first give a respectful reminder. Example: "Thr. Jane, please remember that we need to wash our hands again after cleaning the client's feet."
If the issue is serious, the person refuses correction, it keeps happening, it affects clients, or it requires leadership attention, then escalate.
The objective is not to "catch" colleagues. The objective is to protect the standard.

sections.title: 10. Escalation Route
paragraphs: Escalation should normally follow the appropriate leadership structure. Depending on the nature of the issue, this may include Therapist Guide (TG), Lead Therapist (LT), Supervisor (SP), Client Manager (CM), Staff Manager (SM), and Manager.
The correct escalation point depends on the issue.
Massage technique / routine clarification: usually begin with TG → LT → SP as appropriate.
Client service concern: may involve CM → SP → Manager depending on seriousness.
Staff/team issue: may involve LT / SP → SM → Manager depending on the issue.
Serious or urgent concern: may bypass normal levels where necessary.
The purpose of hierarchy is not to make escalation difficult. It is to ensure that the appropriate leader handles the appropriate issue.

sections.title: 11. Do Not Bypass Leadership Unnecessarily
paragraphs: A therapist should not automatically take every minor issue directly to the Manager when an appropriate leader can resolve it.
For example: If the TG can clarify a massage technique, there may be no need to begin with the Manager. This protects leadership order, efficiency, accountability, and faster resolution.

However, where the immediate leader is involved in the complaint, the therapist does not feel safe escalating to that person, the matter is serious, or the concern remains unresolved, the therapist may appropriately escalate to the next level.

sections.title: 12. Urgent Escalation
paragraphs: Some matters should be escalated immediately.

Examples include threats, violence, serious client misconduct, injury, serious safety issue, serious privacy breach, sexual harassment or inappropriate sexual behaviour, theft, serious damage, serious allegation, and any situation where continuing could cause harm.
In an urgent situation: PROTECT → STOP WHERE NECESSARY → INFORM → ESCALATE IMMEDIATELY.
Do not wait until the end of the shift.

sections.title: 13. The Escalation Procedure
paragraphs: When escalating, therapists should follow this process.

sections.title: Step 1 — Identify the Issue
paragraphs: Ask: What exactly has happened? Separate facts, feelings, assumptions, and opinions.
Your feelings may be valid, but the person receiving the escalation needs to understand the actual situation.

sections.title: Step 2 — Determine Whether Immediate Action Is Required
paragraphs: Ask: Is a client affected? Is anyone unsafe? Could the problem become worse quickly? Does something need to stop immediately?
If yes, take the appropriate immediate protective action and escalate.

sections.title: Step 3 — Do What Is Within Your Responsibility
paragraphs: Where appropriate, take reasonable action first. For example: Correct a small room issue. Replace an available towel. Clarify a simple misunderstanding. Politely restate a client boundary.
Do not unnecessarily escalate something that can be safely and properly resolved immediately.

sections.title: Step 4 — Know When to Stop Trying to Solve It Yourself
paragraphs: If your attempt is unsuccessful, the issue is outside your authority, the matter is becoming worse, you are uncertain, you need a decision, the issue requires documentation, or a standard breach is serious — escalate.

sections.title: Step 5 — Identify the Right Person
paragraphs: Determine: Who has responsibility for this issue? For example TG, LT, SP, CM, SM, or Manager.
Do not simply tell random colleagues.

sections.title: Step 6 — State the Facts
paragraphs: A good escalation should explain: What happened? When did it happen? Who was involved? What have you already done? What is still unresolved? What assistance or decision do you need?

sections.title: Step 7 — Be Solution-Oriented
paragraphs: Where possible, suggest a practical option.
Example: "SP, Client Sam requested something outside our professional service. I explained the boundary, but he repeated the request. I have paused the session and need assistance."
This is much more useful than: "SP, Client Sam is a problem."

sections.title: Step 8 — Follow the Instruction Given
paragraphs: Once the appropriate leader gives a reasonable instruction within their authority: listen, clarify if necessary, carry it out, and report back where required.
Do not escalate for guidance and then ignore the guidance.

sections.title: Step 9 — Follow Up
paragraphs: An escalation is not always complete because the first message was sent.
Where appropriate, confirm: Was the issue resolved? Is another action required? Does the person need an update? Does it need documentation?

sections.title: Step 10 — Learn and Prevent Recurrence
paragraphs: After resolution, ask: Why did this happen? Can it happen again? Is there something we should change?
Escalation should help the organization become better, not merely resolve one incident.

sections.title: 14. A Simple Escalation Format
paragraphs: Therapists can think: ISSUE → ACTION → BLOCKER → NEED.
Example: "LT, I am having difficulty with the pressure sequence in this routine. I have reviewed it and practised it, but I am still unsure about the transition. Please can you guide me?"
Example: "CM, Client Sam is unhappy with the waiting time. I have apologized and explained that we are preparing the room, but he is requesting compensation. I need you to handle the request."
Example: "SM, Thr. Jane and I had a disagreement about today's assignment. We attempted to clarify it but have not resolved it. I would like your help so it does not affect our work."
This keeps escalation clear, factual and useful.

sections.title: 15. Escalation vs Gossip
paragraphs: The difference is very important.

items.label: Escalation
items.body: Goes to someone who can help; has a purpose; seeks resolution; uses facts; is confidential where appropriate; protects standards; ends when resolution is reached.

items.label: Gossip
items.body: Goes to unnecessary people; creates conversation; seeks reaction; often includes assumptions; spreads information; can damage relationships; often continues after the issue is resolved.

sections.closing: A useful question is: "Am I telling this person because they can help resolve the issue?" If the answer is no, consider whether the conversation is necessary.

sections.title: 16. What Good Escalation Looks Like
paragraphs: Good escalation is early, appropriate, factual, calm, responsible, solution-oriented, confidential, and followed through.

Do not wait unnecessarily. Tell the right person. Explain what happened. Do not exaggerate. Explain what you have already done. Make clear what assistance is needed. Share only with those who need to know. Ensure the matter reaches resolution where appropriate.

sections.title: 17. What the Opposite Looks Like
paragraphs: The opposite of the Zura Spa Escalation Standard includes several patterns.

sections.title: Hiding Problems
paragraphs: The therapist knows something is wrong but says nothing.

sections.title: Waiting Until the Problem Becomes Serious
paragraphs: The therapist sees an issue developing but only reports it after a client complains or something goes badly wrong.

sections.title: Gossiping Instead of Escalating
paragraphs: Everyone knows about the issue except the person who can actually solve it.

sections.title: Complaining Without Reporting Properly
paragraphs: The therapist repeatedly says "Nobody is doing anything" but has never communicated through the appropriate channel.

sections.title: Guessing Instead of Asking
paragraphs: The therapist does not understand a routine but proceeds based on assumptions.

sections.title: Taking Unauthorized Action
paragraphs: The therapist personally makes decisions that belong to management.

sections.title: Emotional Escalation
paragraphs: The therapist reports a matter while shouting, insulting, exaggerating or trying to recruit people to their side.

sections.title: Weaponizing Escalation
paragraphs: The therapist constantly escalates minor interpersonal matters simply to punish colleagues, embarrass someone, gain advantage, create trouble, or retaliate after disagreement.
That is not professional escalation.

sections.title: Escalating Without Attempting Reasonable Resolution
paragraphs: The therapist refuses to handle any normal responsibility and immediately reports every minor inconvenience. That is avoidance, not escalation.

sections.title: Bypassing the Appropriate Leader Without Reason
paragraphs: This creates confusion and weakens leadership accountability.

sections.title: 18. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate Failure to Escalate
paragraphs: Failure to escalate can affect far more than the person who stayed silent.
A hidden problem can become a client complaint, a safety incident, a conflict, a financial loss, a damaged relationship, repeated misconduct, a service failure, or a reputational problem.

Zura Spa will therefore not normalize hiding important issues, ignoring serious breaches, failing to report client concerns, concealing mistakes, allowing blockers to remain unresolved without communication, watching serious standards being violated and remaining silent, or guessing when clarification was available.
A problem you responsibly communicate can be managed. A problem you deliberately hide cannot be managed until it is discovered.

sections.title: 19. Why We Will Not Tolerate Misuse of Escalation Either
paragraphs: Escalation must also not become a weapon.

Zura Spa will not tolerate therapists who constantly report colleagues maliciously, exaggerate issues, make false accusations, deliberately remove context, escalate out of revenge, spread the issue after already escalating it, try to create sides, or continually bypass reasonable direct communication where appropriate.
The escalation system exists to solve problems, not create them.

sections.title: 20. Impact of Poor Escalation on the Team
paragraphs: Poor escalation creates surprises, distrust, spreading poor standards, resentment, harder problem-solving, gossip culture, overloaded responsible team members, and damaged leadership structure.

When issues are hidden, leadership may only discover them after significant damage has occurred. If team members repeatedly hide problems or mistakes, colleagues stop trusting information they receive. A behaviour that is never raised may eventually be interpreted as acceptable. A therapist may remain offended for weeks without communicating the issue. Leadership cannot solve problems they do not know exist. If therapists talk sideways instead of escalating upward, workplace information spreads without resolution. When one therapist fails to report blockers early, another therapist may later have to urgently correct the consequences. Constantly bypassing leaders unnecessarily can make roles unclear and reduce accountability.

sections.title: 21. Impact on the Client
paragraphs: Poor escalation may result in an unresolved complaint, continued inappropriate behaviour, poor pressure or service because the therapist was unsure what to do, delayed sessions, unsafe equipment remaining in use, unprofessional conflict becoming visible, a client feeling ignored, or a preventable service failure.
The client should not suffer because "Nobody wanted to say anything."

sections.title: 22. Impact of Good Escalation on the Team
paragraphs: Good escalation creates faster problem resolution, better leadership visibility, greater trust, fewer surprises, better accountability, stronger adherence to standards, more effective training, better support for therapists, safer client experiences, fewer unresolved interpersonal issues, and a culture where asking for help is normal.
A strong team is not a team that never has problems. It is a team where problems reach the right people early enough to be solved properly.

sections.title: 23. What Therapists Should Do
list: Speak up when something requires attention.
Ask when they do not understand.
Explain what they have already done.
Say clearly what assistance they need.

sections.title: 24. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Continue a questionable situation simply because they are afraid to ask.
Wait until an issue becomes a crisis.
Tell everybody except the person who can solve the issue.
Ignore the guidance received after escalation.
Continue spreading the matter after it has been appropriately handled.
Allow unresolved conflict to affect clients.

sections.title: 25. Correction and Accountability
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: Not understanding + asking for clarification = responsibility. Making a mistake + reporting it early = accountability. Encountering a blocker + asking for assistance = problem-solving. Observing a concern + responsibly escalating = professionalism.

But: Deliberately hiding an important problem = performance concern. Concealing a serious incident = serious conduct concern. Repeatedly ignoring serious standard breaches = performance concern. Making knowingly false escalations against another person = serious disciplinary concern. Using escalation maliciously = disciplinary concern.
The purpose of accountability is to ensure that the escalation system remains safe, credible and useful for everyone.

sections.title: 26. The Zura Spa Escalation Standard
paragraphs: NOTICE → ASSESS → ACT → COMMUNICATE → ESCALATE → FOLLOW UP → LEARN

Every therapist should ask: What has happened? Is the client affected? Is anyone unsafe? Can I responsibly resolve this? Do I need clarification? Is this outside my authority? Who is the right person to tell? What have I already done? What help or decision do I need? Has the issue actually been resolved?
DON'T HIDE IT. If it matters, communicate it.
DON'T GUESS. If you do not understand, ask.
DON'T GOSSIP ABOUT IT. Take it to someone who can help.
DON'T REACT EMOTIONALLY. Communicate facts.
DON'T OVERSTEP YOUR AUTHORITY. Know when leadership must decide.
DON'T WAIT FOR A CRISIS. Raise concerns early.
DON'T ESCALATE TO PUNISH PEOPLE. Escalate to seek resolution.
DON'T JUST DROP THE PROBLEM. Follow it through appropriately.
We escalate not because we cannot handle responsibility, but because responsible people know when the right person needs to be involved.
SEE IT. CLARIFY IT. SOLVE WHAT YOU CAN. ESCALATE WHAT YOU SHOULD. FOLLOW THROUGH. PROTECT THE STANDARD.

remember: Raise problems while they are still manageable. Solve what you can; escalate what you should.
